extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of geometry and history of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for composing, analysing and editing Euclid-style geometric propositions and editions: formal parts of a proposition, use of constructions, postulates and common notions, ordering and grouping of propositions, and principles for translations and printed presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal divisions of a proposition
rubrics_metrics.description: In its completest form a proposition contained six parts: (1) the enunciation (problems stated in general terms), (2) the setting-out (kath' ekthesin) stating particular data usually shown in a figure, (3) the specification/definition (siopiasfios) restating what is required in terms of the particular data, (4) the construction (kataskeuh) — additions to the figure necessary for the proof, (5) the proof (dwsei??is), and (6) the conclusion (synperasma) reverting to the enunciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three parts are always found: the enunciation, the proof and the conclusion. Some formal divisions may be absent in particular cases (e.g. IV.10 lacks setting-out and definition). The particular figure is only an illustration and conclusions may be stated generally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Siopiafios (definition/specification and criterion of possibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: The siopiafios serves either as the definition/specification (restating what is required in terms of the particular data) or as a criterion of the conditions of possibility (a statement of necessary conditions for the problem to be possible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both kinds begin with the words 'Set Srj' (translated as 'thus it is required' for definitions and 'thus it is necessary that...' for criteria). Example: I.22 ('Out of three straight lines ... to construct a triangle: thus it is necessary that two of the straight lines taken together in any manner should be greater than the remaining straight line'). Use the siopiafios to state possibility conditions before attempting constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis, synthesis, and reductio (methods of proof and discovery)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Elements is synthetic in exposition, proceeding from the known to the unknown; analysis (reducing the unknown to the known) is primarily a method of discovery and does not appear in the exposition except when used and then normally placed between the definition and the construction. Reductio ad absurdum is a form of analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a proposition is worked out by analysis followed by synthesis, put analysis between definition and construction. Treat reductio as a legitimate analytic technique (called 'reduction to the impossible' in Greek) used in Euclid and elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cases, objections, porisms and lemmas
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposition may have several cases (exikrisis) depending on arrangements of the figure; objections (evatlparia) may be anticipated; a porism (porisma) corresponds to what we call a corollary — an incidental result revealed in a demonstration; a lemma (hypothesis/subsidiary proposition) is a subsidiary statement convenient to assume and sometimes proved later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great geometers usually give one case and leave others to commentators or pupils, but they were aware of other cases. Porisms can be either incidental corollaries or substantive propositions (see Euclid's Porisms). Lemmas may be assumed temporarily and marked to be proved 'in due course'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions: provisional character and pitfalls
rubrics_metrics.description: Many Definitions are open to criticism: some seem original (e.g. of a straight line, of a plane surface), some assume the existence of the thing defined (e.g. square), and some insert theorems into definitions (e.g. definition of diameter includes that it 'bisects the circle'). Some definitions (oblong, rhombus, rhomboid) are never used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid definitions that assume existence of the defined object; avoid embedding theorems within definitions; prefer definitions that serve as provisional statements pending construction-based existence proofs. Be wary of including traditional terms that are unused in the development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postulates 1–3: construction postulates (existence and uniqueness implications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Postulates 1–3 are commonly regarded as the postulates of construction: (1) to draw a straight line joining two points, (2) to produce a straight line in either direction, (3) to describe a circle with a given centre and distance. They assert possibility of drawing and, implicitly, the existence of straight lines and circles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these postulates to justify constructions and existence-claims in proofs. Recognize that Postulates 1 and 2 imply uniqueness properties (e.g. two straight lines cannot enclose a space; two straight lines cannot have a common segment) which render certain axiomatic statements unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postulate 4: all right angles are equal (invariance/homogeneity principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Postulate 4 states that all right angles are equal. It should be placed before the Parallel Postulate because right angles must be determinate magnitudes for the Parallel Postulate to serve as a criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat Postulate 4 as equivalent to the invariability of figures or the homogeneity of space; although it might be provable as a theorem, its proof would require an antecedent invariability assumption. Place it early in foundations when developing Euclidean theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postulate 5: the Parallel Postulate (criterion for intersection and parallels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Postulate 5 provides a criterion by which to judge whether two straight lines in a figure will or will not meet if produced; it is the basis for the theory of parallel lines and necessary for many constructions that depend on intersection points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Postulate 5 both as a constructive criterion (to determine intersection behaviour in figures) and as the foundational axiom for theorems about parallels; be aware that Euclid might assume certain intersections provisionally in early propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common Notions: scope and genuineness
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the Common Notions there is reason to believe only about five are genuine: the first three and two others ('Things which coincide ... equal' and 'The whole is greater than the part'). Some Common Notions (e.g. the one about coincidence) are geometrical and on Aristotelian grounds should not be axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between genuine axioms and generalizations from particular inferences; avoid treating geometrical equality (coincidence) or whole/part relations as primitive axioms without justification — they may have been later insertions into Euclid's text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructions as proofs of existence
rubrics_metrics.description: Construction is used as a method of proving existence in the Elements: constructing an equilateral triangle (I.1), bisecting angles and segments (I.9, I.1), erecting perpendiculars (I.11), and constructing triangles from given sides (I.22).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claiming existence of a figure, provide an explicit construction; place such constructive propositions before later results that depend on their existence. Constructions serve both to illustrate and to prove existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordering of propositions by dependency and pedagogical need
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions are ordered so that earlier ones supply constructions, criteria or results required for later propositions (e.g. I.1 precedes 2, 9, 10, 11; Proposition 20 provides the Stopkr/ios needed for the problem in 22).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing a treatise or text, order propositions to respect logical/pedagogical dependencies — prove possibility/criteria and necessary constructions before posing dependent problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grouping of propositions for thematic and logical flow
rubrics_metrics.description: Book I's propositions fall into three groups: (1) Propositions 1–26 (triangles, perpendiculars, single-triangle theorems), (2) 27–32 (theory of parallels and angle-sum theorem), (3) 33–48 (parallelograms, areas, Pythagorean theorem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize material into coherent thematic blocks (e.g. constructions/triangles, parallels, area theory) to clarify progression and to group closely related results for teaching and reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric algebra (Book II) and algebraic identities by figure
rubrics_metrics.description: Book II specializes in rectangles and squares and uses the gnomon to express geometric equivalents of algebraic identities (e.g. distributive law, (a+b)^2 expansions). Propositions in Book II correspond to algebraic manipulations and solutions of quadratic equations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use geometric figures (rectangles, gnomons) to represent algebraic identities and to solve equations geometrically; show area correspondences explicitly in figures to parallel algebraic formulae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation and edition quality criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Features used to assess translations/editions include independence of translation (from Greek vs Arabic), literalness or liberalization, clarity, whether proofs or enunciations are rearranged, and inclusion of scholia/notes. Examples: Athelhard keeps Arabic terms; Gherard's translation is word-for-word from an Arabic manuscript with Greek words retained; Campanus follows Athelhard closely in enunciations but differs in arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate translations by fidelity to source text, clarity for the target readership, editorial additions or omissions, and the handling of technical terms (whether to retain source-language terms or substitute vernacular). Note how order (proofs before enunciations or vice versa) affects readability and pedagogical utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed presentation and figures in editions
rubrics_metrics.description: Early printed editions faced the difficulty of reproducing geometric figures. Ratdolt's 1482 edition placed figures in the margins and claimed a method by which 'figures could be produced as easily as letters'; experts debate whether figures were woodcuts or assembled from lines and arcs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For printed mathematical works ensure clear and accurate reproduction of figures (consider margin placement, technique for figure production). Presentation of diagrams materially affects the dissemination and usability of geometrical texts.
